This has saved my butt countless times when I'm on the road. It's light, it works well, but that said they are NOT durable nor should you use one for anything other than putting it in your pocket so you can tighten something down with hand strength. If you put a ton of pressure on it to REALLY tighten something down (e.g., a rear wheel), it may strip the tool. So as travel tools go, it's absolutely great, even for something to do a quick adjustment, but don't go nuts-o with it, there's a limit to how much it can take that is best saved for buying a real wrench in the exact size.

Hex keys can be bought- the 8 is used for some lower-end kickstands, the 6, 5, and 4 are used for threadless and threaded stems, linear pull brakes, and handlebars. It truly depends on the bike; sometimes you can often get away with carrying just a 5 on you for travel, especially if it's a bike from the '90s or earlier- hex keys are used less often on those bikes- most of those bikes' bolts use a standard wrench system rather than hex wrenches.

Just recovered from a throat infection, no fever, just a sore throat and chills. I was wondering why my entire body ached in that time, back, legs, everything. What's the scientific reason?
Part of it comes from the cough. Every time you cough you flex and strain most muscle in your body. So, the more you cough the more soreness you'll experience.
Makes sense, SirPoppyCock. That would explain the back pain because the muscles are connected.

"One task of white blood cells is to repair and rebuild muscle fibres which are damaged from day to day. However, when you have the flu, your immune system diverts the white blood cells from this function to fight off the flu virus, thus leaving your muscles and joints feeling sore and achy.

In addition, white blood cells produce a chemical called cytokines when fighting the infection. This causes inflammation in muscles and joints, resulting in pain in a similar way to mild arthritis or rheumatism. However, this achy feeling is temporary, and once your body has fought off the infection, symptoms of achy joints will ease."
No wonder. I could barely get out of bed to cook food, just lethargic all over. Thanks for such a detailed answer!

When you are sick, your body releases histamine and cytokine. These are chemicals that help fight infections. However, they also affect nearby nerves and make them more sensitive to pain, so it results in an achy feeling. You feel it all over your body because they travel through your bloodstream, and can end up in different places.
In a way, to attack the infection all the resources are sent to one area and the rest of the body suffers
